excerpt: What a social media manager does between posts, how a content calendar is planned, and the replies that turn followers into customers.

body.text: This lesson explains the social media manager's job: the planning, the posting, the replies, and the reporting. You will learn how a week is planned before it starts and why the inbox matters more than the follower count.
Posting is the smallest part of the work. The job is deciding what to say, saying it regularly, and answering the people who respond.
Before you start

items: About twenty minutes.
A phone with the apps the business already uses.

body.text: The week before the week

items: Choose three or four things to say, not fourteen.
Write them down with the day and the time.
Choose one picture or short video for each, in daylight where possible.
Write the caption in the way the business speaks, not in the way an advert speaks.
Prepare the posts in advance, so a busy day does not empty the account.
Leave one slot open for something that happens in the week.

body.text: You will see a simple table with a row for each day and a column for the picture and the caption. That table is the whole plan, and it is more useful than any subscription tool.

body.alt: A phone showing a content calendar with posts planned by day.
body.caption: A week planned on paper or in a note. The plan is the job, and posting becomes the easy part.

body.text: It looks like the job is making things go viral. Most of the value comes from being consistent, answering messages, and posting pictures that a customer can recognise.
What to actually post

items: The work itself: before and after, in progress, finished.
The people: the tailor at the machine, the driver loading the van.
The price or the offer, stated plainly, once a week.
A question that a customer would ask, answered in four lines.
A customer's own words, with their permission.
An announcement about hours, holidays, or a new location.

body.text: None of this needs a studio. A phone, daylight, and one clear subject beat a borrowed camera with a dark room.
Do not worry about the number of followers. A hundred people who can buy from you is worth more than ten thousand who cannot.

body.alt: A person replying to messages at a desk with a phone and a laptop.
body.caption: The replies are the work. A message answered within an hour often becomes a sale, and a message ignored becomes a competitor's sale.

body.text: The replies, and the record

items: Answer within the hour during working hours, even if the answer is we will call you at four.
Keep one saved reply for the three most common questions.
Move a real conversation to WhatsApp or a phone call, where it can be finished.
Note every enquiry in a list: name, need, date.
Follow up once after two days, and once more after a week.
Never argue in public. Answer once, then take it to a private message.

body.text: The enquiry list will show you which posts produce customers. That list is the report, rather than a chart of likes.
Reporting to the owner

items: Report enquiries and sales, not impressions.
Name the two posts that produced the most messages.
Say what you will repeat next month, and what you will stop.
Keep it to one page, or one message on a phone.
Send it on the same day each month, so it becomes expected.
Include one problem that needs the owner's decision.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here is common, and each has a straightforward response.

items: A post gets a rude comment: reply once, politely, and hide the comment rather than arguing.
The account is quiet for a week: post one useful thing rather than three apologetic ones.
An order is lost in the messages: search the inbox by the customer's name, then call.
A customer posts a complaint publicly: answer in public, resolve in private, then thank them.
The owner wants daily posts with no material: explain the cost, and offer three good ones.
Somebody copies the account's pictures: report it to the platform, and add a small mark to future photos.

body.text: Practice
Plan one week for a business you know.

items: Write four posts with a day and a time for each.
Take the photographs in daylight.
Write one saved reply for the most common question.
Start an enquiry list with three columns.
Send the owner a five-line report on what happened.

body.text: You can now see the work behind an account that looks effortless. In the next lesson you will look at design as a trade with its own habits.

excerpt: What a graphic designer actually produces, the brief that prevents three rounds of changes, and the file habits that keep a client for years.

body.text: This lesson describes design work as a trade: the brief, the drafts, the files, and the handover. You will learn what a client is really buying and the habits that prevent endless changes.
A designer solves a communication problem with type, image, and space. The tool matters less than the brief, and most disputes come from a brief nobody wrote down.
Before you start

items: About twenty minutes.
Any design tool, even a free one, if you want to follow along.

body.text: The brief, in six lines

items: Who is the audience, in one sentence?
What should they do after seeing this?
Where will it appear: phone screen, banner, or printed flyer?
What must be included: the name, the price, the phone number?
What style does the client like, with one example they can point at?
When is it needed, and how many rounds of changes are included?

body.text: You will see the project change shape once these six lines are written. Half the arguments in a design job come from a missing answer to question two.

body.alt: A designer's table with colour swatches, printed samples, and a notebook.
body.caption: Swatches and printed samples. A colour looks different on a phone screen, on a banner, and on paper.

body.text: It looks like a designer is paid for a picture. A designer is paid for a decision: what to show, what to leave out, and what the reader should do next.
From draft to file

items: Sketch three rough layouts on paper before opening the tool.
Choose one, and build it at the size it will be used.
Check the text size at arm's length, as a reader would.
Check the contrast between text and background in daylight.
Send one draft with a short note explaining the choices, not three drafts.
Keep the changes inside the agreed rounds, and quote for anything beyond.

body.text: A single draft with a reason gets clearer feedback than five options. Clients choose faster when there is one decision in front of them.

You will see the first printed copy look different from the screen, with colours slightly darker or flatter. That difference is normal, and it is why you print one copy before the full run. Your note to the client should mention it, so nobody is surprised.

body.alt: A printed portfolio showing several design projects on facing pages.
body.caption: Three finished projects with a line about the problem each solved. That is a portfolio, and it beats a folder of random images.

body.text: Handover that keeps the client

items: Deliver the file in the format the client will actually use, usually a PDF or a PNG.
Include the source file when the price included it, and say so in writing.
Name the files clearly: business-name-flyer-a5-final.
Check the printed result once, since screens hide colour problems.
Keep a copy of every version you sent, in a dated folder.
Tell the client which fonts were used, in case they need more work later.

body.text: None of this is extra work. A tidy handover takes ten minutes and produces the referral that brings the next client.
Do not worry about the client asking for changes. Two rounds, agreed in advance, turns a difficult client into a normal one.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is a professional problem with an ordinary answer.

items: The client wants a redesign after approval: quote for a new round, politely.
The printed colours are wrong: the file was in the wrong colour mode for print.
The text is unreadable on a phone: the size was set for a laptop. Test at phone width.
The client supplies poor photographs: say so early, and offer to shoot or source them.
The file will not open at the printer's: send a PDF, which opens anywhere.
The client uses the design without paying: keep the source file until payment, as the agreement states.

body.text: Practice
Design one flyer for a real business, from brief to file.

items: Write the six-line brief with the owner.
Sketch three layouts on paper.
Build one at A5 size with a working phone number.
Print it once and look at it from a metre away.
Hand over a PDF, and keep the source file.

body.text: You can now see design as a trade with rules. In the next lesson you will look at remote work from here, in dollars and in hours.

excerpt: How remote work actually runs from Nigeria: the hours, the payment routes, the equipment that matters, and the habits clients trust.

body.text: This lesson is about working remotely from Nigeria: the hours, the payment routes, the equipment worth buying first, and the habits that keep a client for years. You will learn what remote employers actually check.
Remote work is ordinary work done at a distance. The distance changes the payment, the hours, and the trust, and each of those has a practical answer.
Before you start

items: About twenty minutes.
A way to receive money from abroad, or the intention to set one up.

body.text: The hours

items: Many clients work on a time zone four or five hours behind Lagos.
Their morning is your afternoon, which suits some people and not others.
Agree the overlap hours in writing, usually three or four a day.
Say plainly which hours you are available, rather than pretending to be always on.
Plan around power: charge devices before the overlap begins.
Keep one evening free each week, since remote work expands to fill everything.

body.text: You will see the meeting invitations arrive with two times beside them, yours and theirs. Checking both before accepting prevents most missed calls.

body.alt: A desk with a laptop, headphones, and a notebook for remote work.
body.caption: A laptop, headphones, and a notebook. The equipment that matters most is a connection that works when the meeting starts.

body.text: It looks like remote work means working whenever. Clients trust a predictable window far more than an always-available claim.
Getting paid from abroad

items: Ask how the client pays other contractors, which is usually the fastest route.
Compare the fees: a card payment, a transfer service, and a platform each cost differently.
Check the exchange rate the service uses, not only its fee.
Keep an invoice for every payment, with a number and a date.
Record what arrived in naira, since the rate moves between invoice and payment.
Check what your bank requires for foreign payments, which differs by bank.

body.text: An invoice will show the amount, the currency, the work it covers, and a payment reference. That document is what protects you if a payment is questioned a month later.
You will see the payment land in your account with the sender's name and a reference, which should match your invoice. If the reference is missing, ask for it before the month closes.

body.alt: An invoice on a laptop showing an amount in dollars and a payment reference.
body.caption: A clear invoice with a reference number. Most payment disputes are settled by a document somebody can find.

body.text: What clients check

items: Whether you reply within a day, which is the largest single signal.
Whether you say when something will be late, before it is late.
Whether your work arrives in the format they asked for.
Whether the video call works, including your microphone.
Whether the invoice matches the agreed amount.
Whether you write clearly in short sentences, since most of the job is written.

body.text: None of this needs an office or a generator. A quiet corner, a charged laptop, and a habit of replying within a day covers more than equipment does.
Do not worry about the accent or the background. Clients care that they understood you and that the work arrived, and both are within your control.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is common in remote work, and each has a plain fix.

items: The payment is held by the service: check the name on the account matches the invoice exactly.
The rate dropped before payment: quote in the currency you are paid in, where possible.
The call keeps dropping: use audio only, which survives a weak connection.
Power cuts during work: charge in advance and keep a phone hotspot ready.
The client disappears mid-project: keep the unpaid work undelivered until payment.
The hours expand into the night: agree the overlap and close the laptop afterwards.

body.text: Practice
Fix the two things clients notice first.

items: Write your available hours, in their time zone, in one line.
Create an invoice template with a number and a reference.
Test your microphone on a call with a friend.
Set up a payment route and check its fee on a small amount.
Decide which evening of the week stays free.

body.text: You can now work across a border without guessing. In the next lesson you will put a price on your work without apologising for it.

excerpt: How to work out a price from your hours and costs, how to quote in writing, and what to say when a client asks for a discount.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to price your work: work out your real cost per hour, build a quote, and answer a request for a discount without lowering your value. You will leave with a figure and a sentence to say out loud.
A price is not a guess about what somebody will pay. It is your costs, your time, and a margin, written down so you can repeat it.
Before you start

items: A notebook and a calculator.
Your monthly costs, even roughly.
About twenty minutes.

body.text: Find your hourly floor

items: Add your monthly costs: data, transport, power, software, and a share of rent.
Decide the monthly income you need, and add twenty per cent for the quiet months.
Divide by the hours you can actually bill, which is often twenty a week, not forty.
The result is your floor, and no job should be priced below it.
Add the time for revisions, calls, and travel, which people forget.
Round up, since a price that ends in a neat figure is easier to say.

body.text: You will see the floor is higher than expected, and that is normal. The figure includes the hours nobody pays for, which is the reason freelancers undercharge.

body.alt: A notebook with a price calculation and an invoice being written.
body.caption: Costs, hours, and a margin, written down. A price you can explain is a price you can defend.

body.text: It looks like a low price wins the job. A price below your floor wins the job and loses the month, and the client who pays least often asks for most.
Quoting in writing

items: State the work included, in a short list.
State what is not included, such as extra pages or a third revision.
State the price, the deposit, and the payment date.
State the delivery date, and what you need from the client to meet it.
State the number of revision rounds.
Ask for a written yes, even a message, before starting.

body.text: A quote of six lines prevents most disputes. The client who reads it knows what they are buying, and the ones who argue were going to argue anyway.
You will see the client's reply arrive as a short message, often just okay. That single word is the agreement, so keep the quote beside it in the same thread.

body.alt: A phone showing a short written quote with a price and a delivery date.
body.caption: A quote that fits on one phone screen gets read. A long proposal gets postponed.

body.text: When they ask for a discount
You can lower a price by removing something, and you can hold a price by explaining it. What you cannot do is apologise for it.

items: Say the price once, plainly, without a question at the end.
If they ask for less, offer less work rather than less money for the same work.
Offer a payment plan rather than a discount, where the problem is timing.
Name what the price includes, which answers the unspoken question.
Decline politely if the figure is below your floor, and leave the door open.
Never explain a price with an apology, and never call it small.

body.text: None of this needs confidence you do not have. A sentence written down and said slowly works better than a clever argument.
Do not worry about losing the client. A client who will not pay your floor costs you the work you could have done for somebody who will.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is common in a first year of charging, and each has a plain answer.

items: You quoted too low: finish this job, and raise the price for the next client.
The scope grew: point to the quote, and price the extra as a new line.
The client pays late: ask for the deposit before starting the next job.
They compare you with a cheaper quote: compare the work included, not the figure.
You feel embarrassed saying a number: write it down and read it aloud once before the call.
The price is right but nobody buys: the offer is unclear, rather than the price being high.

body.text: Practice
Write one number and one sentence.

items: Add your monthly costs on paper.
Divide by the hours you can bill, and add a margin.
Write your floor in the front of the notebook.
Write a six-line quote for a real job.
Say the price out loud once, without adding a question.

body.text: You can now name a price and stand behind it. In the next lesson you will build the proof that makes the price believable.

excerpt: What belongs in a portfolio, how to show work you did before you had clients, and the three projects that answer an employer's real question.

body.text: This lesson builds a portfolio: the proof that you can do the work. You will choose three projects, describe the problem each solved, and present them in a way that survives a ten-second look.
A portfolio answers one question: can this person do the job I need done? Everything in it should serve that answer, and everything else should be removed.
Before you start

items: Three pieces of work, finished or nearly finished.
A folder on a computer, or a free page online.
About an hour.

body.text: Three projects, three jobs

items: One that shows the core skill of the job you want.
One that shows you finished something with a real constraint, such as a week or no budget.
One that shows you solved a problem for a person, not only made something attractive.
Each with a line saying what the problem was.
Each with a line saying what you did.
Each with one line saying what changed afterwards, where you know.

body.text: You will see the portfolio get stronger as you cut. Six weak pieces make an employer doubt all of them, and three strong ones make the choice easy.

body.alt: Printed portfolio pages laid out on a table with three projects.
body.caption: Three projects, each with a problem and a result. The story around the work is what separates a portfolio from a folder of pictures.

body.text: It looks like you need paid clients before you can have a portfolio. A finished piece for a family shop, with the problem written down, does the same job.
Work without clients

items: Redesign an existing business page you can see is weak, and explain what you changed.
Build a small tool for a problem in your own household.
Volunteer one piece for a church, a school, or a market association.
Copy the structure of a real project, with your own subject and data.
Document the process in three screenshots, which shows how you work.
Ask the person you helped for two sentences you can quote.

body.text: None of these need permission. The constraint is honesty: say plainly that it was practice, and show what you did.

body.alt: A cloud folder with neatly named project folders and files.
body.caption: Named folders, one per project. A recruiter who can find the file in ten seconds is a recruiter who reads it.

body.text: Presenting it

items: Put the strongest project first, since most people read only one.
Use large images, since small screenshots look like clutter.
Write in short sentences, and keep each description under forty words.
Add a link that works without a login.
Test the link on a phone before sending it.
Include a way to contact you, on every page.

body.text: Do not worry about the portfolio looking simple. Simple and working beats elaborate and broken, and a link that opens on a phone is the whole test.
You will see the page load in a few seconds on a phone, with the first project visible without scrolling. If it needs a login, or images take ten seconds, fix that before sending it anywhere.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is fixable in an evening, and none of them needs starting over.

items: The link needs a login: change the sharing settings, then test from another device.
The images are blurred: use the original files rather than screenshots of screenshots.
You have only one project: add two exercises from a course, labelled as practice.
Nobody replies: the first project does not match the jobs you apply for. Replace it.
An employer asks for the source files: keep them, and share only what the job needs.
Your work was used without payment: keep dated copies, which is your proof.

body.text: Practice
Assemble three projects this week, and cut everything else.

items: Choose three pieces, one for each job above.
Write a problem line and a result line for each.
Put them in one folder or one page, strongest first.
Test the link on a phone.
Send it to one person and ask what they understood.

body.text: You can now show proof rather than promise. In the next lesson you will take a first paid client from the first message to the final invoice.
